opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it forced me to think much more carefully before writing anything. When you have a compiler, it's very easy to fall into a loop of writing something half-baked, running it, seeing what breaks, and patching it. That's fast, but you're kind of outsourcing your thinking to the machine. On the iPad, there was no safety net. I had to simulate the program in my head: trace through the loops, check the boundary conditions, think about what happens when the input is empty or huge. If I got it wrong, I wouldn't find out until much later, so I really had to get it right the first time.

That built a habit that's stayed with me. Even now, when I'm writing infrastructure code or debugging something in a large training system, I try to reason about the whole thing first, and understand the logic and the invariants, before I touch the keyboard. It also made me appreciate writing clean, simple code, because when you're tracing it by hand, any unnecessary complexity just hurts you immediately.

And there was a practical side too. It meant I could practice anywhere, on the bus or in a spare moment, without needing a full setup. So it was a small constraint, but it turned out to be really good training for precision and for actually understanding what my code does, rather than just hoping it works.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it started out of necessity rather than any grand plan. When I was younger I didn't always have access to a proper machine, and the iPad was what I had. So I'd write code in a plain notes app, no syntax highlighting, no autocomplete, and definitely no compiler to tell me when I'd made a mistake.

What that forced me to do was actually simulate the program in my head. I had to trace through every loop, keep track of every variable, think about what the memory looked like, because there was no feedback loop to lean on. If you can't run it, you have to understand it. And that turned out to be a much deeper kind of understanding than I'd have gotten by just hitting run and patching whatever broke.

The other thing it taught me was to slow down before writing anything. Normally you type, run, see red, fix, repeat. On the iPad, every mistake was expensive, because I might not find out about it for hours or even days until I got to a real computer. So I started planning more carefully, thinking about edge cases up front, and writing code I was genuinely confident in rather than code I hoped would work.

Later, when I did competitive programming and then research work, that habit paid off a lot. You get much faster at reasoning about correctness, and you debug mostly by reading rather than by printing everything. I wouldn't tell everyone to go throw away their compiler, but I do think there's real value in occasionally removing the safety net and seeing how well you actually understand what you're writing.
